To solve the problem of bitter espresso, one should first check the shot time and grind size [1]. If the shot time is too long, it may indicate channeling, a very dark roast, or water that is too hot [1]. In this case, adjusting the grind size can help [1]. A finer grind can slow down the shot and reduce bitterness, while a coarser grind can speed up the shot and increase bitterness [1].

Additionally, the temperature of the water can also affect the bitterness of the espresso [1]. Hotter water extracts faster, which can lead to over-extraction and bitterness [1]. To mitigate this, running a few seconds of water through the group head before each shot can help bring the temperature down [1].

The beans themselves can also contribute to bitterness [1]. Very dark roasts tend to be more bitter than light roasts, and stale beans can taste flat and bitter [1]. Using beans with a roast date on the bag and consuming them within a few weeks can help minimize bitterness [1].

Other factors, such as uneven tamping, clumpy grounds, and dirty equipment, can also cause bitterness [1]. Ensuring that the basket and group head are clean and well-maintained can help prevent this [1].

In summary, the causes of bitter espresso can be complex and multifaceted, but by adjusting the shot time, grind size, water temperature, and using fresh, high-quality beans, one can help minimize bitterness and achieve a more balanced and enjoyable espresso experience [1].
